Attribute Limit
children.html:
Level Attribute Point Cap
1 3

The simplest way to roll a d2 is by rolling your favorite die, counting an odd roll as a 1 and an even roll as a 2. Ie, you can roll 1d6, treating 1, 3, and 5 as 1, and 2, 4, and 6 as 2.

When you roll a d2 in Tandem with another Modifier Die, be sure to use a different sized die for the d2 so you don't get them confused.

Each Attribute Point beyond 6 add +1 to Checks with that Attribute. When something refers to the number of points you have in a given Attribute, it will use the symbol of that Attribute. For example, heavy armor allows you to add your Points (Vigor Points) to your character’s AC.

There is a limit to how high your Attributes can be, determined by your level. The limit starts at 3 points, and rises with your level as shown in the table below.

children.html:
In BtP, five Attributes represent your capabilities as an individual, described to the right.

Attributes are measured in Attribute Points, each of which increases the size of your Mod Die (short for Modifier Die) for that Attribute, as shown in the table below. An Attribute with 0 points has no Mod Die.

children.title: Checks & Modifiers
The d20
children.html: You will typically roll a d20 anytime a Check is called for. This roll represents what Fate feels the result should be. Rolling a 1 on the d20, referred to as a Natural 1, is especially damning. Rolling a 20, referred to as a Natural 20, represents outstanding success.

children.title: Modifier Dice & Types of Checks
children.html:
When making a Check, the activity being performed determines the Mod Die you will use. There are four types of checks, described below.

  • Attack Checks are made when you attempt to harm a specific creature or object. For example, swinging a weapon.

  • DC Checks are special Checks made when you attempt to affect an area, forcing one or more other entities to make a Save Check.

  • Save Checks are made when you attempt to avoid a dangerous situation or effect, such as a trap or a hostile spell.

  • Skill Checks are made when you attempt to do anything not covered by the previous Checks, such as lifting a log, recalling knowledge, or interpreting body language.

children.title: Rolling in Tandem
children.html: Many facets will allow you to roll two Mod Dice in Tandem, meaning you roll both and use the higher number as the value of your Mod Die for that Check. If one and only one of the Mod Dice is negative, instead subtract that die's result from the other.

children.title: Advantage & Disadvantage
children.html:
You will sometimes roll a Check with Advantage or Disadvantage, representing a situation in your favor, or against you.

Advantage
means you roll two d20s and take the higher value for that Check.
Disadvantage
means you roll two d20s and take the lower value for that Check.

Multiple effects granting Advantage or Disadvantage to a Check do not stack; a Check either has Advantage, Disadvantage, or neither. Having both Advantage and Disadvantage cancels both, no matter how many instances of either are being applied.

fields.Advantage: means you roll two d20s and take the higher value for that Check.
fields.Disadvantage: means you roll two d20s and take the lower value for that Check.

children.title: Bolstered & Hindered
children.html:
When facet or effect says your Check is Bolstered or Hindered, that means you increase or decrease the size of the largest Mod Die for that Check by a number steps equal to the Bolstered or Hindered level, respectively. Bolstered and Hindered levels subtract from each other, so if a Check would be Bolstered 2 and Hindered 1, the Check is Bolstered 1 as a result.

For example, if you make an Attack Check with a d10 Mod Die that is Bolstered 2, you would roll a d12 for the Mod Die and add 1 to the Check Total. If you make a Save Check with a d4 Mod Die that is Hindered 4, you would reduce the size of the Mod Die by 4 steps, down to a -d4.

If multiple effects would add Bolstered or Hindered levels, add their levels together. If a Check would be Bolstered past a d12 Mod Die, add the remaining Bolstered levels to the Check Total. If a Check would be Hindered past a -d12 Mod Die, subtract the remaining Hindered levels from the Check Total.

children.title: Empowered & Weakened
children.html:
Certain circumstances or effects may cause your Checks to be Empowered or Weakened, increasing your chance of success or failure, respectively.

Empowered
means you either roll an extra d4, adding the result to the value of your Mod Die (not the Check Total), or if the Check is being rolled in Tandem with two Mod Dice that are both d4s or larger, add their results together for the value of your Mod Die.
Weakened
means you roll an extra d4 and subtract the result from the value of your Mod Die.

Like Advantage and Disadvantage, multiple effects causing a check to be Empowered or Weakened do not stack, and they cancel each other out.

fields.Empowered: means you either roll an extra d4, adding the result to the value of your Mod Die (not the Check Total), or if the Check is being rolled in Tandem with two Mod Dice that are both d4s or larger, add their results together for the value of your Mod Die.
fields.Weakened: means you roll an extra d4 and subtract the result from the value of your Mod Die.

children.title: Step 1: Apply Modifiers
children.html: After the PM calls for a Check, identify any effects that would cause it to be Empowered, Weakened, or made at Advantage or Disadvantage. If the Check is Bolstered or Hindered, adjust the size of your Mod Die.

children.title: Step 2: Roll the Dice
children.html: Roll your d20 alongside any Mod Dice you have for the Check.

children.title: Step 3: Calculate the Check Total
children.html: Add the value of the d20 to the value of your Mod Die. The result is your Check Total. Rarely, you may have other modifiers to apply at this stage, such as excess Bolstered levels.

children.title: Steps 4: Compare to the DC
children.html: Announce your Check Total to the PM, who compares it against the DC (Difficulty Class) of the Check. The DC varies depending on what the Check is for. If your Check Total is equal to or greater than the DC, your character Succeeds. You might already be aware of the DC, or you may have to ask the PM if you Succeeded. DCs are often purposely hidden to elevate suspense at the table.

children.title: Step 5: Measure your Success
children.html: Success and Failure don't end at the DC. When a Check Total is 5 or more above or below the DC, the result of the Check is often greater than a normal Success or Failure.

children.title: Attack Checks
Weapon Attack Checks
children.html: Weapon Attack Checks refer to Attack Checks made with a weapon, most commonly with the Strike Action. The DC of a Weapon Attack Check is usually the target's AC.

children.title: Spell Attack Checks
children.html: Spell Attack Checks refer to Attack Checks called for by a spell. Spell Attack Checks are usually made against an Attribute of the target, meaning the DC equals 10 plus the Attribute Points the creature has for that Attribute.

When your PC attempts a harmful action against a specific entity, they will make an Attack Check. The Mod Die you use and the DC for the Check are determined by the kind of attack you are making. For example, a Gladiator attacking with a longsword would use their Martial Die against the AC of their target, while an Arcanist casting a spell would use their Arcana Die against one of the target’s Attribute DCs (10 plus the target’s Attribute Points). The result of an Attack Check is usually damage being dealt to something.

Beating the DC of an Attack Check by 5 or more is called a Deadly Success, while failing by 5 or more is called a Complete Failure.

children.title: DC Checks
children.html: When your PC does anything that affects an area (called an Area of Effect, or AOE) such as casting a spell that makes a line of flame, they will make a DC Check, which is a special Check made by rolling only your Mod Die, then adding 10 to the result. Each affected creature then makes a Save Check using the Attribute specified in the effect. DC Checks can have Advantage or Disadvantage for the purpose of other effects, such as Radiance, but are unaffected by those modifiers.

children.title: Save Checks
children.html:
When your PC is targeted by a harmful effect or faced with a dangerous situation, such as a giant boulder falling from the ceiling, they will make a Save Check. A Save Check always specifies the Attribute it targets, meaning you use that Attribute’s Mod Die as the Mod Die for the Check. When you make your character, the Class you choose will list certain Attribute Save Checks you can roll in Tandem with your Class Die.

The DC of a Save Check is determined by the effect that caused it. Beating the DC of a Save Check by 5 or more is called a Complete Success, and often results in avoiding any harmful effects entirely, while failing by 5 or more is called a Deadly Failure, with deadly effects to match.

children.title: Skill Checks
Attribute Skill Checks
children.html: When your PC performs an action based solely on their mental or physical capability, you will make an Attribute Check. The PM determines the Attribute you will use, such as asking for a Perception Check to spot a tiny object. When you make an Attribute Check, use your Attribute Die as the Mod Die for that Check.

children.title: Basic Skill Checks
children.html:
Basic skill checks are made when your PC attempts to do something that most people can learn without specialized instruction or significant trial and error. A Basic Skill Check is always made with two Attribute Dice rolled in Tandem. For example, if you attempt to hide from a guard, the PM can ask you to roll a Tandem / check, representing how fast you find acceptable cover and how well you conceal yourself from sight.

In the table above you’ll find Attribute combinations that cover many common PC endeavors.

children.title: Trained Skill Checks
children.html:
Trained skill checks are only made when a PC attempts to perform an action that one of their Hobbies or Professions allows them to do. They are made by rolling your Mod Die for the relevant Hobby or Profession in Tandem with the Mod Die of the most relevant Attribute for the Check. For example, if you have the Fisherman Profession and you are trying to catch a fish, your PM can ask for a Tandem Fisherman/ Check, representing your experience as a fisherman and your ability to feel when you have a bite.

Skill Checks involving your class are also considered Trainined Skill Checks, and use your Class Die in Tandem with an Attribute Die.

When your PC tries to interact with the world in any way not covered by the other Checks, they will make one of the three types of Skill Checks: Attribute, Basic, or Trained. The DC of a Skill Check is determined by the PM, as are the effects of Success and Failure, including Complete Success and Complete Failure, if your roll at least 5 above or below.

children.title: Critical Failure
children.html: Rolling a Natural 1 on any Check is a Critical Failure, causing the Check to be Weakened.

children.title: Critical Success
children.html:
Rolling a Natural 20 on Check means you score a Critical Success. Critical Successes have different effects depending on the type of Check, as detailed below, but scoring a Critical Success always restores one expended Radiance.

Weapon Attack Checks
that score a Critical Success inflict a Condition based on the type of damage dealt, as described in the Strike Action.
Spell Attack Checks
that score a Critical Success are automatically a Deadly Success, and the spell’s level increases by 1 when resolving the Deadly Success effects.
Save Checks
that score a Critical Success are an automatic Complete Success, and the effects of that Complete Success for the creature become nothing, no matter what they would have been.
Skill Checks
that score a Critical Success have the value of their Mod Die set to the maximum value.

When your character attempts to affect the world in a way that success is not guaranteed, such as attacking a creature, picking a lock, or even cooking an omelette, the PM will call for a Check. Checks are executed in the order below.

  1. Identify any modifiers to your Check.

  2. Roll a d20 and the relevant Mod Die, if you have one.

  3. Add the numbers together.

  4. Compare the Check Total to the DC.

  5. Determine the result.

  6. Resolve the effect.

children.title: Hobbies & Professions
Hobbies
children.html: A Hobby is a single activity that your PC became capable of through practice in their spare time. Each Hobby has a corresponding Mod Die that you roll as the Mod Die for any Skill Check you make using that Hobby.

children.title: Professions
children.html: In addition to their Hobbies, your PC also has one or more Professions. A Profession is the occupation your character had before becoming an adventurer; what they did to make money or otherwise survive. Professions can provide access to a wide array of potential Skill Checks, and they allow your character to make money during Downtime.

Your PC's skill at each of their Hobbies and Professions is measured by their Rank, which determines the size of their Mod Die. Starting at level 3 and every odd level after, you can increase the rank of one of your Hobbies or Professions by one step, or you can become a Novice in a new Hobby. The highest rank you can have in either is limited by your level, as shown below.

children.title: Guidelines for Hobbies & Professions
Choosing Hobbies
children.html:
When deciding on your PC's Hobbies, keep the following in mind.

  • Specific. Hobbies should be written down on your character sheet as a specific activity, usually in gerund form (ending in "-ing").

  • Amateur. Having a Hobby implies that your PC is practiced at that activity, but not to the degree that they could monetize it successfully.

  • Narrow. When choosing a broad activity, such as reading or art, you must narrow it down to a specific genre or category. For example, "Nonfiction Reading" or "Oil Painting".

  • Weapon Training. When you gain a Hobby, you can choose to replace it with the training to wield a specific weapon, such as a longsword or a flail.

children.title: Choosing Professions
children.html:
When deciding on your PC's Professions, keep the following in mind.

  • Official. Professions should be written down on your character sheet as formal occupations, such as "Blacksmith", "Farmer", or "Accountant".

  • Sustaining. Having a Profession means your PC has all the skills required to make money or otherwise feed themselves with their given profession.

  • Broad Experience. A PC with the "Fishing" Hobby may be able to catch and identify a fish, but a PC with the "Fisherman" Profession can catch fish, read weather patterns, understand deck logs, identify fish diseases, and any number of other things required to run a fishing business.

  • Logical Training. If you choose a Profession that would naturally grant you an ability to wield weapons or wear armor, such as “Soldier”, your PM will decided which weapons and armor you gain the training to use. You don’t add your Class Bonus to your AC unless your Class is what allows you to wear your armor.

children.html: You can choose almost anything for your Hobbies and Professions, so long as your PM agrees to it. Horseback riding, smithing, sleight-of-hand, basket weaving, anything! You can also work with your PM to identify some Hobbies that may be relevant to the adventure ahead. Infinite options can be daunting however, so a list of backgrounds are provided later in this document for inspiration or ready-made selection.

Rather than a static list of skills such as athletics or stealth, BtP uses Hobbies and Professions to represent the skills your PC has, gained from what they did to survive and thrive before their adventuring career.

When a PC attempts something that requires specific, intentional instruction or practice (i.e. picking someones pocket, riding a horse, translating a language, or recalling specialized information), they must have exposure to that activity or information through one of their Hobbies or Professions in order attempt a Skill Check. If they don't, the PC has no chance of succeeding in the way they would like to.

children.title: Actions
{AP} Action Points (AP)
children.titleHtml: Action Points (AP)

children.title: Temporary Action Points
children.html: Some facets can grant temporary , which is not constrained by your maximum and typically disappears at the end of the turn.

When you roll Initiative, you gain equal to your Maximum, which is 5 in most cases. You can perform Actions on your turn by spending as listed in the Action’s Cost. You regain expended at the end of your turn.

Outside an Encounter, you generally don’t track .

children.title: Reactions & Triggers
children.html: When an Action's cost includes the Reaction tag (for example “Reaction, 1 ”), it will also list a Trigger. Triggers can be any set of circumstances, and you can only use a Reaction when the Trigger occurs. You can only use one Reaction in response to a given Trigger, even if you have multiple Reactions that share the same Trigger.

children.title: Consecutive Action Penalty (CAP)
children.html: Many Actions have a stacking penalty if they are used multiple times in the same turn, known as a CAP (Consecutive Action Penalty). The CAP of an Action can vary, but the most common is a Basic CAP, meaning the Action costs an additional 1 for each time it has been used that turn (0 on the first use each turn).

children.title: Subsequent Actions
children.html: When an Action requires you to perform another Action as part of its execution, you don’t spend for the subsequent Action. However, you can't take an Action if you can't perform its subsequent Actions. For example, being Restrained prevents you from taking Move Actions, meaning you can't take any Action that tells you to Strike or Stride.

children.title: Improvised Actions
children.html: If you want your PC to do something not covered by an existing action, the PM will arbitrate if its possible, the you need to spend, and what kind of Check you need to make.

children.title: Action Categories
Exclusive Categories
children.html:
The categories listed below are only available to certain classes. Your class will tell you which categories it grants you access to.

  • Arcane Actions are available to those that manipulate Light with their own power.

  • Combat Actions are available to those trained in combat.

  • Supernatural Actions are available to those capable of evoking Light from other entities.

Each Action lists one or more categories that may affect how they function or are responded to, detailed below.

  • Basic Actions are available to all creatures.

  • Concentrate Actions require focus to execute.

  • Hostile Actions will be seen as a sign of aggression to non-Allied creatures.

  • Manipulate Actions involve touching or moving objects.

  • Move Actions involve moving the body a significant amount.

  • Secret Actions are rolled by the PM on behalf of the Player, so that the Player does not know the result.

When you want to interact with the world or story, you do so by having your PC take an Action. Actions are things your PC can do that have defined rules. Most Actions have a Cost, usually measured in (Action Points, or AP). You must spend the listed in an Action’s cost to perform it. Some Actions have Requirements you must meet to use them as well.

children.html: Actions are available to those capable of evoking Light from other entities.
Below are rules for each Action your PC can take.

children.title: Exploration
Brightness
Full Brightness
children.html: While in Full Brightness, such as daylight or a well-lit room, you can see normally. Sources of Full Brightness emit double their radius in Low Brightness.

children.title: Low Brightness
children.html: While in Low Brightness, such as an enclosed space lit by a candle, your Checks that rely entirely on sight have Disadvantage unless you have Night Vision.

children.title: Darkness
children.html:
While in Darkness, such as night under an open sky, you are considered Blinded for any Check you make in relation to something that is also in Darkness, unless you have Night Vision. You are only Blinded for the purposes of those Checks however, and do not suffer the other effects of the Blinded Condition.

You can perceive areas within your line of sight according to the brightness level of that area.

children.title: Absolute Darkness
children.html: In Absolute Darkness, such as a sealed chamber with no light sources, all creatures that rely on sight to perceive their environment are Blinded.
There are four levels of brightness that determine how well you can see: Full Brightness, Low Brightness, Darkness, and Absolute Darkness.

children.title: Visibility
Clear Visibility
children.html: Clear Visibility means nothing is impacting visibility in your environment, and you can see as normal.

children.title: Low Visibility
children.html: Low Visibility is caused by things like heavy fog or rain. While in Low Visibility conditions, you cannot visually sense anything beyond twice your Radius.

children.title: Minimal Visibility
children.html: Minimal Visibility is caused by extreme conditions such as sandstorms, raging blizzards, or intense whipping rain. While in Minimal Visibility conditions, you cannot visually perceive anything beyond your Radius, and within your Radius, you can only see the silhouette of creatures and objects. Attack Checks against the of creatures in areas of Minimal Visibility have Advantage, while Attack and Save Checks made by those creatures have Disadvantage.
Sometimes other factors such as fog or intense rain may also impede your ability to see. There are three levels of visibility: Clear Visibilty, Low Visibility, and Minimal Visibility.

children.html: An object is any physical entity that is not a creature. They have stat blocks just like creatures, and can be targeted in the same way. All objects share statistics from the stat block below, and will not repeat information that does not vary based on its characteristics. Objects do not have a level, and their is based on their Material and Size.
Different environmental factors can affect how you interact with your surroundings.

children.title: Encounters
Initiative
Surprise
children.html: If the PM determines that any participant in the encounter is taken by surprise, that creature has Disadvantage on their Initiative Check.

children.title: Tied Initiative
children.html: If two PCs tie in their Initiative, the one with the larger Mod Die (counting Bolstered and Hindered levels) will go first. If their Mod Dice are the same size, the PCs will decide amongst themselves who goes first.

An Encounter (most commonly a fight) begins when the PM calls for Initiative. When they do, you roll a special check, called an Initiative Check. The result of this check determines when you take your turn relative to other creatures in the Encounter.

children.title: Acting in an Encounter
children.html:
To perform an Action during an Encounter, you must spend (Action Points). When you roll Initiative, you gain equal to your maximum (5). You regain all spent at the end of your turn. Most Actions can only be performed on your turn. Actions with the Reaction tag in their Cost can be performed any time their Trigger occurs.

Actions and are explained in depth in the Actions section of this document.

Movement Types

Name Description Associated Attribute
Burrow Digging through loose ground.
Climb Climb vertical surfaces without a Check. or
Fly Flying through the air. or

rows: Climb vertical surfaces without a Check.

children.html:
Some facets will give you the ability to move in different ways, like in the air, water, or up vertical surfaces. Each additional movement type you gain will have its own base Movement value. Like your regular Movement, this is increased by your total points each point of one of your Attributes, though not necessarily (+1 at 1, +2 at 2, etc).

Whenever a rule or facet refers to your Movement without specifying a type, it is referring to your normal movement, which is how far you can move along the ground. Your PM may allow you to use a different movement type for the effect.

There are five movement types beyond normal ground movement, listed in the table below.

children.title: Treacherous Terrain
children.html:
The PM may declare that particularly difficult, unstable, or narrow terrain is considered Treacherous Terrain. Moving into or out of a space considered as Treacherous Terrain consumes 2 spaces of Movement.

For example, if you attempt to cross a narrow ledge, or move through a knee deep river, you would need to expend 2 Movement for every space you travel. If you only have 1 Movement left, you can’t move into or out of Treacherous Terrain.
Movement is a resource that determines the number of spaces you can travel on the ground when you take the Stride action. Outside of an Encounter, your Movement is doubled when Striding.

children.title: Falling
Landing on a Creature or Object
children.titleHtml: Landing on a Creature or Object
children.html: If you land on something after falling, and the fall would deal damage, you and the thing you fell on take half the damage you would have taken. If the thing you fell on has Crushing Resistance, you take the amount of damage resisted by it.

When you begin falling, you immediately fall 5 spaces. For every 1 spent while falling, you fall another 5 spaces plus the last amount of spaces you fell after the Action or effect you spent on resolves.

For example, if you begin falling on another creatures turn, you will immediately fall 5 spaces. If you then spend 1 to Interact with a piece of your equipment, you will fall 10 spaces once that Action is resolved. If you spend another 1 to do anything else, you will fall 15 spaces. If you then spend 2 on a single action, such as Interacting with something else, you will fall 20 spaces, then 25 spaces.

The next time your turn ends, if you have fallen less than 100 spaces since the end of your last turn, you fall the remaining amount of spaces it would take to get you to 100. If you are still falling, you immediately fall another 5 spaces at the start of the next turn, and the cycle repeats. You can only fall a maximum of 100 spaces before the end of each of your turns.

When you fall more than 1 space, you take crushing damage equal to the number of spaces you fell upon landing. If you are Prone when you fall, roll a d20. On a 1, the damage you take is doubled. On a 20, it is halved.

children.title: Moving on a Grid
Spaces
children.html: Each point where lines intersect represents a space. When you move from one space to another, you do so by moving along any of the lines connecting your current space to an adjacent space.

children.title: Range
children.html: When measuring the range between two entities, start counting from a space adjacent to one of the entities and stop counting in the space occupied by the other using the shortest route.

children.title: Size
Large Creature Spaces
children.html:
Size Spaces (Radius)
Large 1
Gigantic 2
Enormous 3
Gargantuan 4
Colossal 5
Titanic 6

The PM can increase the size radius of Titanic creatures past 6 as they see fit.

All creatures and objects have a Size, which affects how many spaces they take up on a grid. Most PCs will be Medium or Small, but other creatures can get much larger or smaller. Medium and smaller creatures only occupy one space, and multiple Tiny and Miniscule entities can occupy the same space.

On a triangular grid, each Size above Medium occupies all spaces adjacent to those occupied by the next-smallest Size. This allows the spaces occupied by each Size to be measured via radius from their center space, as shown in the table below.

children.title: Juking
children.html:
When moving on a triangular grid, if you have at least 5 Movement, you can hop across the line between two spaces (the base of any triangle formed with your space as the top) to the space in straight line from your current position. This is known as Juking, and only costs 1 space of Movement.

You can Juke once each time you take a Move Action that allows you to move. You can Juke even if there are Hostile creatures occupying the spaces at both ends of the line you move through, but you can't Juke into or out of Treacherous Terrain.
BtP uses a triangular grid for Encounters. If your PM uses this grid, use the following rules.

children.title: Damage
Halving
children.html:
Damage is often halved based on the result of a Check. Spells typically deal half damage on a Failed Attack Check or Successful Save Check. If you would add your Mod Die to a damage amount that was halved, it is usually added after doing so, unless otherwise stated by the effect.

Damage is the most common thing to be halved, but in general, the default rule when halving anything in BtP is to round up. Any effect that needs to round down will say so specifically.

children.title: Immunity
children.html: Entities can have Immunity to one or more damage types. If something would take damage of a type it has Immunity to, it instead takes no damage. Entities can also have Immunity to Conditions. If you would gain a Condition you are immune to, you instead don't, though you can still be targeted by effects that cause the condition.

children.title: Resistance
children.html:
Most entities have Resistance to one or more damage types. Damage Resistances have a level, and each time something takes damage of a type it has Resistance to, the damage is reduced by that level. For example, if a creature with Thermic Resistance 3 takes 5 Thermic damage, it would be reduced by 3, and the creature would take 2 damage. Resistances to the same damage type from different sources add together.

Entities can also have Resistance to Conditions, which work similarly and reduce the level of the received condition by the level of their Resistance to it.

children.title: Vulnerability
children.html: Some entities have Vulnerability to one or more damage types. Damage vulnerabilities are displayed with a die value. Each time something takes damage of a type it has Vulnerability to, the Vulnerability Dice are rolled and added to the total damage taken. For example, when a creature with Arctic Vulnerability 1d4 takes Arctic damage, the damage is increased by 1d4.

When a creature takes damage, their Endurance is reduced by the amount of damage taken. For example, if a creature with 12 Endurance takes 5 Thermic damage, they will have 7 Endurance remaining. Effects that deal damage will usually state the exact amount of damage the target takes based on the result of a Check. You will then often add the value of your Mod Die to that number, as with Striking with a Weapon. Damage always has a type, and when a creature or object would take damage, you first have to apply any Immunity, Resistance, or Vulnerability the target has to the damage types being dealt.

children.title: Cover
Light Cover
children.html:
Light Cover gives you Advantage on , , and Save Checks, so long as the cover is between you and the origin of the effect forcing you to make the Check. Attack Checks made against you also have Disadvantage if there is Light Cover between you and the attacker.

Light Cover includes things like large fallen logs, benches, and overturned tables. Allies in a direct path between you and a Hostile creature also count as Light Cover if they are no more than one size smaller than you.

children.title: Full Cover
children.html:
Full Cover gives you an automatic Complete Success on , , and Save Checks, so long as the cover is between you and the origin of the effect forcing you to make the Check. Attack Checks made against you are also an automatic Complete Failure if there is Full Cover between you and the attacker.

Full Cover is anything sturdy enough to blunt an impact that completely obscures your PC from a source of harm.
There are two tiers of cover that you can take advantage of during an Encounter, Light Cover and Full Cover. The PM determines what counts as cover and what doesn’t.

children.title: Areas of Effect
Circle
children.html: Listed as "X-space circle", each creature on the ground within X spaces of the space chosen as the center of the circle will be affected.

children.title: Cone
children.html: Listed as "X-space cone", each creature between two straight lines, each X-spaces long and 60 degrees apart starting from the cone's origin will be affected. A visual representation of a 3-space cone at different orientations is shown below. Creatures in the red-dotted spaces would not be affected.

children.title: Cylinder
children.html: Listed as "Cylinder (X-space radius, Y spaces high)", effects with this area behave as as an X-space circle, but creatures in the circle no more than Y spaces above the origin space are also affected.

children.title: Emanation
children.html: Listed as "X-space emanation", creatures within X spaces of the emanation's origin in any direction will be affected. Emanations are persistent and move with their origin.

children.title: Line
children.html: Listed as "X-space line", each creature in a line drawn X spaces from the origin space will be affected. Some effects will require the line be straight, but others can create lines the connect any sequence of adjacent spaces.

children.title: Sphere
children.html: Listed as "X-space-radius sphere", each creature within X spaces of the origin space in any direction will be affected.
Many things can create an Area of Effect, causing multiple creatures to be affected at once.
When time is of the essence, you will enter the Encounter mode of play. During an Encounter, you will track how you spend on your turn and between it.

children.title: Radiance
children.html:
Radiance is a resource that represents the light within your PC, and how brightly it shines. Your PC starts with 1 Radiance and gains an additional Radiance for every 2 points they have. You regain spent Radiance equal to half your points when you finish a Long Rest. When you score a Critical Success on any Check, you regain one spent Radiance. If you have all your Radiance, you can immediately use that Radiance on the Check, before determining the result.

You can spend Radiance to do one of the following.

  • Advantage. Gain Advantage on any Check you make.

  • Empower. Empower any Check you make with Advantage, including one you spent Radiance to gain Advantage on.

  • Unconventional Skill Check. Use a Hobby or Profession for any Skill Check, regardless of how relevant it would be.

  • Bonus Damage. Deal bonus damage on a Weapon Attack equal to the weapon's Deadly DV.

children.title: Endurance and Vitality
Endurance
Temporary Endurance
children.html:
Many effects can grant you Temporary Endurance, which you track separate from your regular Endurance. Notably, when you finish a Long Rest, you gain Temporary Endurance equal to your Points times your Class Bonus.

When you take damage, reduce your Temporary Endurance first if you have any. Temporary Endurance lasts until you finish your next Long Rest, unless the effect that granted it states a duration. If you ever gain Temporary Endurance while you already have some, choose whether you keep your current amount or gain the new amount, including the new duration. Temporary Endurance never stacks.

Endurance represent your PC's ability to keep functioning under high stress situations. Your PC's Endurance is gained from their Class. When your PC is dealt damage, the damage is subtracted from their current Endurance.

children.title: Vitality
children.html: Your PC's physical body and how close they are to death is represented by your Vitality, which starts at 3. If your Vitality ever drops to 0, you die. Vitality is lost when you take damage while at 0 Endurance. The amount of damage doesn't matter, if you take damage with 0 Endurance, you lose 1 Vitality.

children.title: Dying
children.html: When you lose Vitality, you gain the Dying Condition with a level equal to the amount of Vitality you are missing. Dying forces you to make Survival Saves, described below. If your Endurance is above 0 while Dying, you also take Somatic damage equal to twice your Dying level at the start of your turn. Somatic Resistance cannot reduce this damage below 1. You can Stabilize yourself on your turn to attempt to reduce your Dying level. The Dying condition is also removed entirely when you regain any Vitality.

children.title: Survival Saves
children.html:
When your Endurance hits 0, and when you start your turn with the Dying condition, you must make a special Save Check referred to as a Survival Save. The DC for a Survival Save equals 10 plus your Dying level.

If you have any Endurance when you make a Survival Save, you do so at Advantage.

Success
You fall Unconscious.
Complete Success
Your Dying level reduces by 1, and you wake up if you are Unconscious, so long as another effect is not keeping you Unconscious.
Critical Success
As a Complete Success, and you regain 1 Endurance if you have none.
Failure
You fall Unconscious and your Dying level increases by 1.
Deadly Failure
You fall Unconscious and lose 1 Vitality. After gaining the Dying condition from losing your Vitality, your Dying level increases by 1.
Critical Failure
As a Deadly Failure, but you lose 2 Vitality instead of 1.

children.html: Life and death in BtP are managed by Endurance and Vitality. These together represent the overall state of your PC's health, and your ability to keep moving.

children.title: Resting
Short Rests
children.html:
A Short Rest is achieved when your PC spends 10 minutes without performing an Action that costs more than 1 . At least 5 minutes must also be spent occupying the same space in a resting position (sitting, leaning against a wall, etc).

When your PC finishes a Short Rest, they gain the following benefits.

  • Vitality. They regain missing Vitality equal to half their points (remember, always round up in BtP).

  • Facet. Uses Any facets that state they regain uses or are otherwise refreshed on a Short Rest are restored.

  • Endurance. You can spend Rest Charges to regain Endurance equal to half your Endurance Maximum. Your PC has a number of Rest Charges equal to their maximum Vitality.

A PC can only benefit from two Short Rests per Long Rest, and not within an hour of each other.

children.title: Long Rests
Heroic & Gritty
children.html: The Resting Rules are the easiest way to modify the stakes and difficulty of your game. The rules to the left are the default, Heroic rules. If you want a Gritty game, remove regaining Vitality on a Short rest, and reduce the Vitality regained on a Long Rest to 1 or half the PC's points, whichever is higher.

A Long Rest is achieved when your PC spends at least 6 hours sleeping and 2 hours without performing an Action that spends non- resources.

When your PC finishes Long Rest, they gain the following benefits.

  • All Endurance. They regain all missing Endurance.

  • Temporary Endurance. They gain Temporary Endurance equal to their points times their Class Bonus.

  • Rest Charges. They regain all spent Rest Charges.

  • Vitality. They regain missing Vitality equal to 1 plus half their points.

  • Radiance. They regain spent spent Radiance equal to half their points.

children.html: When your PC is low on resources, you can take a Rest to regain strength.

children.title: Damage Types
Crushing Piercing and Slashing (Rank 1)
children.html:
Crushing, Piercing, and Slashing together represent the ‘physical’ damage types. Most weapons deal one or more of these damage types, as do most physical hazards.

Crushing damage is dealt by anything that inflicts blunt-force trauma. Falling from high place, getting hit with a hammer, and being squeezed by a giant snake are all examples of Crushing damage. Rarely, Crushing damage can inflict the Bruised condition.

Piercing damage is dealt by anything that goes into its target. Arrows, rapiers, spike traps, and fangs all deal Piercing damage. Rarely, Piercing damage can cause a target to lose Vitality.

Slashing damage is dealt by anything that cuts the target, such as a sword, claw, or other edged hazard. Rarely, Slashing damage can inflict the Bleeding condition.

children.title: Arctic and Thermic (Rank 2)
children.html:
Arctic and Thermic damage represent damage dealt by the transfer of kinetic energy.

Arctic damage is dealt by anything that rapidly removes heat, such as Ice or Frost spells. Environments of extreme cold will likely contain hazards that deal Arctic damage as well. Arctic damage often inflicts the Freezing condition.

Thermic damage is dealt by anything that rapidly adds heat, like Fire or Flame spells. Hazards involving extreme heat, such as pools of lava, also deal Thermic damage. Thermic damage often inflicts the Burning condition.

children.title: Psychic and Somatic (Rank 3)
children.html:
Psychic and Somatic damage affect the soul and flesh of a creature, respectively. Anything that lacks a soul is immune to Psychic damage, while anything inorganic is immune to Somatic damage.

Psychic damage is dealt by effects that attack the mind or spirit of a creature, such as Ethereal creatures or telepathic attacks.

Somatic damage is dealt by anything that directly compromises flesh, such as poison and blood loss. Effects that wither flesh also deal Somatic damage.

children.title: Caustic and Galvanic (Rank 4)
children.html:
Caustic and Galvanic damage represent the subtraction and addition of matter at a molecular level.

Caustic damage is dealt by anything that physically dissolves material. Being drenched in acid or a highly basic solution would both deal caustic damage, usually with the Dissolving condition.

Galvanic damage is dealt when there is a massive transfer of electrons into the target, most often with lightning. Galvanic damage can rarely cause the Paralyzed condition.

children.title: Cosmic, Chthonic, and Sonic (Rank 5)
children.html:
Cosmic, Chthonic, and Sonic damage represent the philosophical concepts of all that is above, below, and about, respectively. They are expressions of the fundamental forces that make up the Prismos.

Cosmic damage is dealt by exposure to unfathomable truths. Gaining forbidden knowledge, seeing the unseeable, and other eldritch events can induce this damage type. Cosmic damage often inflicts the Morphing condition.

Chthonic damage is dealt by exposure to the chaotic presence of the underworld. Being supernaturally subjugated, defaulting on an underworld deal, and the general presence of Infernal Light all deal Chthonic damage, which can also inflict the Possessed Condition.

Sonic damage is dealt by intense material force. The pressure wave of an explosion, conjurations of Temporal Light, and highly-magnified sound waves are all sources of Sonic damage. Sonic damage often inflicts the Stunned Condition.

children.title: Divine and Profane (Rank 6)
children.html:
Divine and Profane damage are the rarest damage types, representing the enforcement and corruption of universal law, respectively.

Divine damage is dealt by effects utilizing Platinum Light to rebuke the very existence of their target. Divine damage can induce a variety of Conditions, though Blinded is common.

Profane damage is dealt from powers granted by elder beings outside the Prismos, corrupting the form and soul of their target. Profane damage can also cause many Conditions, though lose of Vitality is common.

BtP has fourteen damage types, categorized by rarity into ranks. Higher ranked damage types are more rare, and Immunity and Resistance to a given damage type becomes less common the higher it’s ranked. Most damage types have a Condition associated with them.

children.title: Conditions
Condition Level & Multiple Instances
children.html:
Some Conditions have a level (noted with an X by their name) which increases the potency of the condition. When a creature is afflicted with a Condition it already has, it takes the higher level between the two. Condition levels are never added together.

For example, if a creature is Burning 3 and gets hit by a Fire spell that inflicts Burning 1, it is still only Burning 3. If the creature was Burning 1 and the spell inflicted Burning 3, it would become Burning 3.

children.title: Bleeding X
children.html:
You take Somatic damage at the start of each of your turns equal to your level times X. You can spend 5 on your turn to reduce the level of this Condition by 1 if you have a bandage or other suitable item, as determined by the PM.

Immunity to Slashing damage prevents this condition.

children.title: Blinded
children.html:
You can’t see, and suffer the effects below.

Attack Checks
Attack Checks against you have Advantage.
Checks
Your Checks have Disadvantage, and you suffer an automatic Complete Failure on any Check entirely based on sight, as determined by the PM.
Terrain
You treat all spaces as Treacherous Terrain.
Visual Immunity
You are immune to any effect that requires the target to see it.

children.title: Bruised
children.html:
Your flesh is bruised. Your and Checks are Weakened until you finish a Rest.

Immunity to Crushing damage prevents this condition.

children.title: Buffeted X
children.html: Your AC is reduced by X. This condition ends at the start of your turn.

children.title: Burning X
children.html:
You are on fire. You are Numbed X and take 3X Thermic damage when you gain this Condition and at the start of your turn. You and any creature that can touch you may spend 2 on their turn to reduce the level of this Condition by 1. This Condition ends automatically if you are ever submerged in water.

Immunity to Thermic damage prevents this Condition.

children.title: Deafened
children.html:
You can’t hear, and suffer the effects below.

Checks
Your Checks are Weakened, and you suffer an automatic Complete Failure on any Check that depends entirely on hearing, as determined by the PM.
Audible Immunity
You are immune to any effect that requires hearing to affect a target.

children.html:
You are covered in a caustic substance. You take 2X Caustic damage when you gain this Condition and at the start of your turn. The level of this Condition reduces by 1 at the end of your turn. You and any creature that can touch you may spend 1 on their turn to wipe off the substance with cloth or pour non-caustic liquid on you to reduce the level of this Condition by 1. It ends automatically if you are ever submerged in water.

Immunity to Caustic damage prevents this Condition.

children.html: Your Checks are Hindered X.

children.title: Dying X
children.html: You are dying. You take 2X Somatic damage at the start of your turn if your Endurance is above 0 (Somatic Resistance cannot reduce this damage below 1). You and any creature that can touch you may attempt to Stabilize you on their turn to reduce the level of this Condition. It ends automatically when you regain Vitality.

children.title: Exhausted X
children.html:
You are extremely tired, and suffer the following effects:

Hindered
All of your Checks are Hindered X.
Sloppy
Attack Checks against you are Bolstered X.
Slow
Your Movement is reduced by X (this stacks with the Slowed Condition).

The level of this Condition reduces by 1 each time you finish a Long Rest.

Immunity to Arctic damage prevents this condition.

children.title: Immobilized
children.html: You can't move. Your Save Checks are Weakened, and all your Movements are 0. If you are Immobilized because of something physically holding you in place, anything that tries to move you by force must make a Check against a DC determined by what is Immobilizing you. The PM determines the Check and DC.

You are overwhelmed with fear, and suffer the below effects.

Frightened
You cannot move toward the source of your panic.
Overwhelmed
You are Muddled X and Numbed X.
Flight
When you gain this Condition, you immediately Stride as a Reaction and use all of your Movement to flee from the source of your panic.

At the start of your turn you must make a Save with a DC of 10 plus X.

Success

Failure

The movement of your limbs is restricted, and you suffer the below effects.

Open

Restricted

Stuck

children.title: Stunned X
children.html:
You are momentarily stunned. Any Reaction you take costs an additional X . During your turn, you can't take Actions, but you can spend to reduce the level of this Condition by 1 per spent.

When you start your turn Stunned, make an Save Check against a DC of 10 plus X if you have an active Sustained effect. On a Failure, you can't Sustain this turn.

children.title: Unconscious
children.html:
You are unconscious, and suffer the below effects.

Incapacitated
You can’t spend .
Vulnerable
Attack Checks against you are Bolstered 10, your and Checks are automatic Complete or Deadly Failures, and all of your other Checks are Weakened.

This Condition ends if you take damage, unless a specific effect is keeping you Unconscious.

sections.html: This document is playtest material for Beyond the Prism, a tabletop roleplaying game. All content is subject to change.

children.title: Character Creation
Envisioning Your Character
children.html:
Sometimes you have an idea for your character's theme or personality before you know anything else about them. You may want to play a scientist, or a gruff bartender-turned-vigilante, or maybe you just want to be 'the strong man'. Maybe you want to be a strong bartender that used to be a scientist but after 'the accident' they stick to mixing drinks.

Whatever your idea, BtP is collaborative story telling game above all else. Your PC's ancestry, background, and class all serve to fulfill the vision you have for them, so take a moment to think through the kind of character you'll enjoy playing most. As you go along, work with your PM to find ways of fitting your PC's life into the story. Whether that means coming in as a complete stranger or having your backstory be a central plot thread, you should both work to make something that is, above all, fun.

children.title: Choosing an Ancestry
children.html: You may want to start with your PC's Ancestry, which is their genetic heritage. There are many sapient species across the facets, such as humans or praedans, each of which come with their own traits. Your PM may decide that not all Ancestries are available to select, so work with them to choose one that best fits your character within the story being told.

children.title: Choosing a Background
children.html:
Your PC's Background represents their life before they became an adventurer, and is comprised of the following.

  • Two Hobbies at Amateur Rank.

  • One Profession at Proficient Rank.

  • One Heritage Facet.

Hobbies and Professions represent the skills your character has acquired up to the point that they became an adventurer, and are used to make Skill Checks other characters may not be able to, as described in the Hobbies & Professions section of this document. Your Heritage Facet represents the advantages gained from the environment they were raised in, be it a loving home with modest income or a brutal war camp where every day was a struggle.

The default suggestion for making a character in BtP is to make your own Background by picking your Hobbies and Profession, then choosing your Heritage Facet. Some pre-made Backgrounds are listed further in this document for inspiration or easy selection.

children.title: Choosing a Class
children.html: The most impactful decision you will make toward fulfilling the vision of your character is their Class. Your PC's class represents the years of effort or exceptional natural endowment that grants them mind or might above other sapients. It will determine their role in your adventure, their abilities, and how they solve problems. You will generally want to discuss class selections with your fellow players and PM to create a balanced party.

children.title: Assigning Attributes
Point Buy
children.html: With Point Buy, you have 12 Attribute Points to distribute between your , , , , and , all of which begin at -1 points. At 1st level, a PC's Attributes can't go above 3 points (you can put no more than 4 Points into any one Attribute). Once you’ve decided how to spread your points, mark down the Mod Die for each of your Attributes, as explained in the Attributes section of this document.

children.title: Rolling
children.html:
To roll for your Attribute Points, roll 5d4. Add the highest four values together, then add 1 to the total. You then assign Attribute Points as you would with Point Buy, using the final amount instead of 12.

For maximum variability, you can also roll 1d4, subtract 1, use that number as your total Points, then do the same for your remaining Attributes.
Some players like to assign Attribute Points first and work up from there. There are two methods for determining your starting Attribute Points. The PM decides which method all the players will use.

Your PC's Alignment to each Light is measured in levels, shown in the table below.

children.html:
As you create your PC, determine your answer to each of the questions below. Your answers will grant you one level of Alignment as shown in the table further below.

Your answers to these questions will also live on your character sheet as a role-playing tool to quickly center yourself into your PC's personality. If you aren't sure how they would respond to something in the story, check your answers!

children.title: Attunement
children.html:
Alignment isn't just a cosmetic personality trait. Certain items imbued with Light, such as a gilded sword inscribed with Fire runes, are known as Arcane or Supernatural items, depending on how they were imbued.

Your character's Alignment will determine the Arcane and Supernatural items your character is able to Attune with. A PC can Attune with any items that match one of their Alignment types, and the strength of their Alignment improves the effects of such items when used.

children.title: Age
children.html:
While your PC can technically be any age, it's recommended only experienced TTRPG players attempt to play a PC younger than 17, unless the player themselves is in that age range.

Otherwise, your PC can be as old as your PM allows. You can simply pick an age and move on, or you can intentionally age-up your character by 10 years to gain an additional two Hobbies and one Profession at Proficient Rank for the cost of 1 , , or Point. You can repeat this process as many times as you like, but it’s not recommended to do so more than twice.

In BtP, Alignment is not a measure of morality. Rather, Alignment measures your PC's resonance with the individual forces of creation, or Lights, described below.

Flame Light is evoked from the heated forges of civilization, fearless ingenuity, and the grit of a soldier.

Frost Light permeates the quiet night air, the icy winds of mountain forests, and the patient gait of a hunter.

Pneuma Light forms the thoughts of sapient creatures, interpersonal connection, and souls of all manner.

Soma Light fuels the flesh of every living creature, from the strength of their muscles to their sensory instincts.

Mordant Light suffuses the salted waves of the ocean, where selfish greed is the only way to survive.

Velvet Light is thunder and passion, bringing lovers together like lightning between storm clouds.

Infernal Light is the fundamental force of power, radiating from the blood of those who let nothing stand in their way.

Lunar Light is all that is known, and all that is not. It is information, deception, and the never-ending cosmic expanse. Every mystery, and every answer.

Temporal Light is the foundation of all that is real. It is the physicality of all things, the balancing force of existence, and the source of life in the Prismos.

Platinum Light is the very essence of creation, pure and unbiased. Ever-shining from the Sun at the apex of the Prismos, all other Lights refract from it.

children.title: Devotion
Primadeus
children.html: Creator god of the Prismos and the source of all Platinum Light. They are depicted as a many-winged, never-ending serpent with a scaled lion's head. Primadeus maintains a neutral disposition, only truly enforcing one thing - that 1 prim is never worth more or less than 1 prim.

children.title: Asmodeus
children.html: Patron god of the ori and the nexus of Infernal Light, often preferring the form of an imposing ori with up-turned horns that are symbolic in ori culture. He both is and is lord of the Infernal Prism, granting favor to the powerful, and power to those who take it.

children.title: Temporia
children.html: Matriarch of the gods and the mundalves, she is the World Prism itself. Her Temporal Light imbues the land with life, and her followers seek to keep harmony among its creatures. With Asmodeus, she gave birth to Mordax and Aurodeus.

children.title: Lunaeus
children.html: Ever-watching enigma from the nadir of the Prismos, and progenitor of the ulu. He is, or is thought to be, the moon, shining Lunar Light upon the facets and rewarding those who seek the unknown. He's also an incorrigible trickster, prodding his followers into mischief. With Temporia, he sired Nixoria and Somaria.

children.title: Mordax
children.html: Filled with hatred for his parents and apathy for almost all of his family, including his daxan spawn, Mordax is the god of spite. His Mordant Light reflects across the ocean waters and in the eyes of those with an axe to grind. His mother's approach brings the Drowning season, said to be her tears at his rejection.

children.title: Velestria
children.html: Blessed and loved child of Nixoria and Pneumax, often depicted as a voluptuous woman of the beholder's ancestry scantily clad in flowers. Mother of the amorous taurtons, her Velvet Light fills the cracking clouds of thunderstorms and the wombs of expectant, and attempting, mothers across the facets.

children.title: Somaria
children.html: Raging twin of the Wild Gods and Great Chiefmother of the corpug tribes. She is the matron of brute force, described as a giantess of rippling muscle clothed in animal pelts. She unlocks the primal potential of mortal flesh with blessings of Soma Light upon warriors who let nothing stop their victory.

children.title: Pneumax
children.html: Guide to both the souls and thoughts of sapient creatures, and father of the cogitani. He was born of Asmodeus' jealous clash with Lunaeus, and brokered peace among the Prismatic Pantheon. His ethereal form permeates the the Soulscape, connecting people with rays of Pneuma Light.

children.title: Aurodeus
children.html: The Daybringer, who forged humans in the ambition of his Flame Light. He grants resolve to the bold-hearted, and fuels the fires of civilization. Temporia visits him each year, bringing the Gold Season.

children.title: Nixoria
children.html: Silent twin of the Wild Gods and Nightmother of the praedan. She steps in tandem with the footfalls of hunters, is warden to the wilderness of the World Prism, and her Frost Light caresses the weary into gentle sleep. She welcomes her mother each year for the Silver Season.

children.title: Gïgeye
children.html: It is said the shadows can hold many terrors, but none more terrifying than the vampyre. Their obluminous lineage is a mystery, but profaned scholars claim in a time before the severing, a gigantic mass of congealed blood consumed a pregnant ori, infecting her child with the first strain of vampyrism.

children.title: Ukthulus
children.html: All that is, is Light. What then, of darkness? In the Void, there can be nothing but death eternal. It cannot be traveled through, as there is nothing to walk upon. How then, does a dead god stir within its umbra?

children.title: The Lady
children.html: What begins, must inevitably end. They did not go unnoticed. Their time will come. She is waiting. She is near.

The Prismatic Pantheon consists of ten gods, each of which govern a different Alignment. A description of each is provided below, along with some more esoteric entities, should you wish to play a character devout to a higher being.

children.title: Step 2. Ancestry Facets
children.html: Write down your ancestry, then go over the facets it grants. Some will further increase your Movement, or grant additional Vitality or Radiance. All ancestries will grant you a level of Alignment. Make these changes to your sheet, and if you'd like you can write down your ancestry facets in the Facets section of your sheet.

children.title: Step 3. Background
children.html: Add the Hobbies from your Background at Amateur Rank, and the Profession at Proficient Rank. Then write down your Heritage Facet in the Facets section of your sheet and apply any bonuses you gained from it to your statistics.

children.title: Step 4. Class
Alignment
children.html: Add the level of Alignment gained from your class, if applicable.

children.title: Armor & Weapons
children.html: In the Armor Training and Weapon Training sections on your sheet, note the types of armor and weapons your character can use.

children.title: Endurance Maximum
children.html: Set your class's starting Endurance as your Endurance Maximum.

children.title: Save Checks
children.html: In the Save Checks section on your sheet, note which Save Checks can be rolled in Tandem with your Class Mode Die. Use a "/" between the Mod Dice for Tandem rolls, or a "+" if the Save Check is Empowered, as with an arcanist's Save Checks.

children.title: Facets & Actions
children.html: In the Facets section of your sheet, write down all of your class's 1st level facets. in the Actions section, write down any special actions you received from your class, with their cost and a brief description.

children.title: Spells & Maneuvers
children.html: If you gained any spells or maneuvers at 1st level, write them down in that section of your sheet, along with the resource to use them. You will keep track of that resource in that section.

children.title: AC (Armor Class)
children.html: While not wearing armor, your AC equals the sum of your highest two Attributes. If you have armor at the start of the story, calculate your AC with the rules in the Equipment section of this document, including your Class Bonus if allowed by your class.
Your class will make the biggest changes to your sheet. Write down your chosen class in the "Class" box, then address the following.

children.title: Step 5. Final Details
children.html: Using the rules earlier in this chapter, answer the questions that define your PC's personal Alignment. Decide if you would like to age-up your character, and if you would like to follow a god. You can also work with your PM to create friends, rivals, or even enemies that connect you to the world of the story being told.

Once you have a firm understanding of the PC you're going to play, its time to fill in your character sheet.

children.title: Experiences
children.html:
Experiences are a form of player reward, given as a result of daring actions, successes, and failures. They are a way to reward players on the spot with a boon that calls back to their triumphs and lessons.

Experiences are usually a single-use boon that grants Advantage on a specific kind of Check, and are named after the success the player achieved. For example, a player that defeats a Large creature may receive the 'Monster Slayer' experience, granting Advantage on a single Attack Check against a Large creature.

Though they normally grant Advantage, the PM can award Experiences with any effect they desire, and can give it multiple uses. However, Experiences in general should not be permanent.

children.title: Levels
Time in Level
children.html:
Level Time-in-Level
1 1 month
2 3 months
3 6 months
4 10 months
5 15 months
6 21 months
7 28 months
8 36 months
9 45 months

The increasing time spent at each level is meant to give narrative weight to them. Reaching level 1 in a class represents either years of hard work and training or exceptional natural ability. If your PC encounters a 10th level Arcanist or Gladiator NPC at 1st level, that means they're about 14 years ahead of where you are, and have spent those 14 years rigorously perfecting their craft.

These timeframes also help enforce the kind of stories meant to be told at each level. Stories in Btp can be loosely split into three tiers: level 1-3, 4-6, and 7-9. Level 10 can either be used as a series climax, epilogue, or Bonus chapter, depending on the story.

Below is a table that shows the scale of threat a monster (or PC) is meant to represent at each level.

Level Threat to a...
-1 Small animal
0 Lone commoner
1 Group of commoners
2 Trained soldier
3 Group of soldiers
4 Village battalion
5 Township
6 Fortified settlement
7 Major city
8 Nation Capitol
9 Unified region
10 Country
11 Multiple countries
12 Continent
13 Plane of existence
14 Multiple planes
15 Minor deity
16 Outer realm
17 Major deity
18 Universe
19 Prime deity
20 Elder Titan

Your PC should never encounter an enemy more than 4 levels above their own. So for stories told from level 1-3, your party will be dealing with threats to individuals, the local populace, and townships, usually within the span of one year. The scale of conflict ramps up from there, as will the stakes of your story and the consequences of your character's actions.

As your PC advances through the story, they will learn and grow, eventually culminating in a Level Up. BtP doesn't have experience points, instead opting for a set of guidelines meant to foster an organic, sensible progression that avoids power spikes and showcases the character's growth over time. The table below shows the time characters should spend at each level across Exploration and Downtime before moving to the next level, but when PCs Level Up is ultimately the PM's decision.

children.title: Prismacasting
Arcanist's Grimoire
children.html: You have authored a book containing five 1st-level arcanum spells, known as your Grimoire. The spells you can add to your Grimoire are restricted by your Arcane Triumvirate.

children.title: Recording Spells
children.html: While you have a written copy of an arcanum, such as in a book or scroll, you can copy the spell into your Grimoire. Doing so takes 4 hours per level of the spell, or half that if its type is taught by your Triumvirate.

children.title: Replacing your Grimoire
children.html: You can spend one week of Downtime to create a copy of your Grimoire. If you Grimoire is ever destroyed, you can create a new one over a Long Rest, recording the spells you had prepared that day into the new one.

children.title: Preparing Spells
children.html: Each Long Rest, you can Prepare a number of arcana from your Grimoire equal to your Arcanist level plus your points, allowing you to cast those spells until your next Long Rest. Spells prepared this way must have a level no higher than your Max Spell Level, as shown in the Arcanist Class Table.

You become aware of arcane effects within your Radius for 10 minutes. During that time, objects, areas, and creatures with arcane effects glow faintly to you, and you can spend 2 to Identify Arcane entities as long as they are within your radius. You cannot Detect Arcane through 1 inch of metal, 1 foot of stone, or 3 feet of wood or dirt.

As an accomplished scholar of the arcane, you have become sensitive to the presence of concentrated prisma. When you Identify Arcane, you can replace your Die with your Arcana Die. You also gain the Detect Arcane Action, described below.

children.title: Arcane Flow
children.html:
Where others see domain and hierarchy, Arcanists see synergy. After Prismacasting a spell, any Checks you make for the next spell you Prismacast before the end of your next turn are rolled in Tandem with your Die if both spells were of different types.

Any Checks you make as part of Surecasting a spell are also rolled in Tandem with your Die.
Practioners of the mystic art known as Prismacasting, Arcanists manipulate the world through sheer knowledge.

Kinetic Specialization
children.html:
As a student of the Kinesis Triumvirate, the spells you discover follow the rules below. Kinesis Arcana are those of the Fire, Ice, and Arc type.

  • Initial Arcana You must choose at least one Kinesis Arcanum of each type for the initial five spells recorded in your Grimoire.

  • Initial Cantrips You learn three cantrips, two of which must be Kinesis Arcana.

  • Level Up When you gain an Arcanist level, you record two arcana into your Grimoire of a level up to your Max Spell Level, one of which must be a Kinesis Arcanum.

  • Bonus Spells At 4th, 7th, and 10th level, you learn an additional cantrip of any type, and you record an additional arcanum of any type into your Grimoire of a level up to your Max Spell Level.

You can Prismacast any Kinesis Arcanum recorded in your Grimoire without spending any Prisma. The spell must have a level no higher than half your Arcanist Bonus, but you don’t need to have it Prepared.

Once you use this facet, you must finish a Long Rest before you can use it again.

children.html:
When you Prismacast a Kinesis cantrip that involves an Attack or DC Check, you can spend an additional 1 . If you do, the Check is Bolstered 1.

You also gain a level of Flame, Frost, and Velvet Alignment.

Specializing in Ice, Fire, and Arc prisma, Arcanists of the Kinesis Triumvirate are masters of manipulating the energy that flows through physical matter. They are among the most destructively potent Arcanists.

Each Arcanist belongs to or once studied under a Triumvirate, a collection of like-minded Arcanists that specialize in the same three prisma types. The teachings of an Arcanist's Triumvirate shape their approach to prismacasting.

Your body is an instrument of destruction, granting you the benefits below.

  • Unarmed Strikes. When you Unarmed Strike, your body has the Pushing property, its DV equals your Points, and its Deadly DV equals twice that amount.

  • Powerful Jump. The height of your High Jump equals 1 plus your points, rather than half your points, and the maximum distance of your Long Jump after moving equals twice your points, instead of 2 plus your points, if it would be larger.

  • Wild Instinct. Your Initiative Checks are rolled in Tandem with your Wild Die.

  • Heavy Weapons. Heavy melee weapons don’t have the Two-Handed property while you wield them.

children.title: Wild Fervors
Roaring Fervor
Roaring Rage
children.html:
Some of this fervor’s facets require you to Roar, releasing a loud shout from the depths of your lungs. Your Rage gains the following additional benefits which require you to Roar.

  • Adrenaline. After taking damage during Rage, you may Roar. If you do, you gain Temporary Endurance equal to your Berserker Bonus.

  • Frenzy. When you make an Attack Check, you may Roar and sacrifice Temporary Endurance up to your Berserker level. On a Hit, the target takes additional damage of a type dealt by the attack equal to twice the amount sacrificed, or three times on a Deadly Hit.

  • Fear. When you Roar, each Hostile creature within an emanation out to your Berserker Bonus is Numbed 1 until the end of your next turn.

Berserkers gain their strength from the depth and power of their emotions. Their Wild Fervor represents an emotion they feel so deeply, it evokes response from the Prismos itself, bolstering their bodies into forces of nature.

The devotion you carry pushes you forward where others would fall. You gain additional Vitality equal to half your Champion bonus, and you roll your Devotion Die in Tandem with your Die for Survival Save Checks.

Also, when you roll a Tandem / Check to persuade someone of anything relating to your Champion’s Cause, you can replace your Die with your Devotion Die for that Check.

children.title: Glorious Exploits
Executing Maneuvers
children.html: To execute a Maneuver, you must expend Will equal to half its level.

Will, in spell’s Cast Time

You cast one of your mantras or Exploit spells at a level up to your Max Exploit Level. Evocations cast this way require no hands.

Reaction, 1

Strike range

Roll your Spell Mod Die in Tandem with your Attribute Die for the Attack Check of your Strike, which gains additional effects determined by your Champion’s Cause.

children.subtitle: Evocation (type varies), 1st-level

children.html: You gain the Decree action and you learn the Smite Evocation as your first Glorious Exploit, both described below.

Your Will resonates so strongly, it bends the Prismos to your aid. You start with a maximum of 2 Will, which you can spend to execute certain Champion facets. Your maximum increases each level, as shown in the Will column of the Champion Class Table. You regain expended Will when you finish a Rest.

You can spend Will to execute Glorious Exploits, which are spells and maneuvers you learn at certain Champion levels as shown in the Exploits Known column of the Champion Class Table. The maximum Exploit level you’re allowed to learn is shown in the Max Exploit Level column on that table as well. The Exploits you can choose are determined by your Champion’s Cause.

children.title: Undaunted
children.html:
Your mission comes before everything, including yourself. On your turn you can sacrifice 1 Vitality (no required) to do one of the following:

  • Press On. You regain Endurance equal to 10 times your Champion Bonus.

  • Overcome. Perform a Glorious Exploit without spending any Will ( is spent as normal). The Exploit is performed at one level above your Max Exploit Level if it's a spell, or two above if it's a maneuver.

You don't begin Dying from sacrificing Vitality this way. Once you use this facet, you must finish a Rest before you can use it again.

children.title: Champion’s Aura
Connection
children.html:
You believe in the power of connection and that only together can progress be achieved.

1st Level You can Assist any creature making an Attack Check within your Aura, and Assisting a creature within your Aura costs 1 less . The assisted creature gains Temporary Endurance equal to twice your Points.

You also gain a level of Temporal Alignment.

children.title: Force
children.html:
You believe that absolute authority is the only way to bring change.

1st Level When you Strike a creature within your aura, you can spend an additional 1 to roll your Die in Tandem with your Attribute Die for the Attack Check.

You also gain a level of Infernal Alignment.

children.title: Subversion
children.html:
You prefer to mislead your opposition and advance your cause in shadow, keeping your true beliefs hidden.

1st Level Your AC gets a bonus against Attack Checks made by creatures within your Aura equal to half your Champion Bonus. When a creature within your Aura forces you to make an Save Check, it’s rolled in Tandem with your Devotion Die.

You also gain a level of Lunar Alignment, and when you roll a Tandem / Check to lie to someone, you can replace your Die with your Devotion Die for that Check.
Champions evoke power from the unwavering devotion to their cause, but each goes about it in a different way. Choose your preferred method of championing your cause from those below.
Fervent believers in a cause beyond themselves, Champions harbor a will so strong that light itself answers their call-to-arms.

children.title: Champion's Causes
The Throne
Infernal Will
children.html:
Strengthened by your own might, when you Succeed on an Attack Check against a creature and when a creature suffers a Failure against your DC Check, you regain Endurance equal to half your Champion Bonus, or your Champion Bonus if the result was Deadly.

If multiple creatures make a Save Check against your DC Check, this facet triggers only for the creature with the highest result.

You also regain 1 spent Radiance when you roll a 19 on the d20 for an Attack Check.

Once you Evoke Submission, you must finish a Rest before you can do so again.

children.title: Throne Exploits
Dominating Smite
children.html:
Your Smite gains the Infernal type, and when you Smite, your Attack Check gains the additional effects below.

Success
2 Chthonic damage.
Deadly Success
3 Chthonic damage, Possessed .
Failure
Chthonic damage.
Complete Failure
Nothing.

children.html: As a Champion of the Throne, you can learn Martial and Psychological Maneuvers, as well as Flame and Infernal Evocations when you gain a new Glorious Exploit. Choose two Exploits to learn when you gain this facet in addition to Smite.
For power, authority, and the rule of the strong. Champions of the throne demand that a greater will is brought forth, and that lesser wills bend the knee.

children.html: You gain the Evoke Darkness action, described below.

children.title: Endwalker
children.html:
The closer you are to the grave, the stronger you become. You contain Darkness equal to your missing Vitality, giving you the following benefits.

  • Movement. Your Movement gains a bonus equal to your Darkness.

  • Damage. Each time you take or deal damage, you can increase or reduce one type of the damage by half your Darkness.

items.name: Movement
items.html: Your Movement gains a bonus equal to your Darkness.
items.text: Your Movement gains a bonus equal to your Darkness.

items.name: Damage
items.html: Each time you take or deal damage, you can increase or reduce one type of the damage by half your Darkness.
items.text: Each time you take or deal damage, you can increase or reduce one type of the damage by half your Darkness.

children.title: Darkness Exploits
Void Smite
children.html:
Your Smite gains the Void type, and when you Smite, your Attack Check is against the target’s and gains the following additional effects.

Success
Divine damage, and the target loses 1 Vitality.
Deadly Success
2 Divine damage, and the target loses 2 Vitality.
Failure
The target loses Endurance equal to its Level.
Complete Failure
Nothing.

fields.Success: {SL} Divine damage, and the target loses 1 Vitality.
fields.Deadly Success: 2 {SL} Divine damage, and the target loses 2 Vitality.
fields.Failure: The target loses Endurance equal to its Level.

children.html: As a Champion of Darkness, you can learn Feral and Martial Maneuvers, as well as Void and Infernal Evocations when you gain a new Glorious Exploit. Choose two Exploits to learn when you gain this facet in addition to Smite.

In darkness, we are all equals. Champions of Darkness serve to push all things towards their natural end, and ward against the evils of immortality and prolonged existence. Everything must end, eventually.

Be it for Justice, revenge, power or glory, a Champion's Cause is their strength, that which they would sacrifice everything for. A Champion's devotion to their cause is so potent, it moves the very World Prism to action.
